items.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: But he was the guy who integrated the Goodman band in 1935 by getting him to hire Teddy Wilson and then Lionel Hampton and then Charlie Christian.

ctx.x: No. That’s what I talk about in my class and that’s where integration — when John Hammond, who I’m sure you know, knew, or know of — well I was lucky enough to know John Hammond. He worked at two labels, Columbia and Vanguard. I worked at two labels, Columbia and Vanguard. And I got to know Mr. Hammond in the 80s. He died in ’87. But he was the guy who integrated the Goodman band in 1935 by getting him to hire Teddy Wilson and then Lionel Hampton and then Charlie Christian. And he told me stories that are just…

items.title: Buckingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2019
items.q: how he talked Benny Goodman into hiring Teddy Wilson and integrated music in 1935

ctx.x: Um hum. So what I was finding was the tape with the splicing, the splices. You know how they have the white splice tape of course. But they would cut right, diagonally. They were professionally edited. But on other reels I started hearing pieces of things. Or I’d hear one that was not edited. And I said I don’t remember that. And I’d start listening and I’d start making — I had tablets filled with notes. And then I started finding reels with — it was spliced but you’d start playing it and it would be like a solo,…

electric guitar and then that would go on for a while and there would be a splice and here’s another solo from a totally different song. It was just solos on these reels, spliced together. And I started listening and it doesn’t take a genius to figure out that’s Lester Young trading off of Charlie Christian. These things. I get chill bumps as you can imagine. So I started — I was literally, I don’t know how many legal pads I filled with notes on this. And I got with Doug Sax and started constructing this stuff.…

Some of his statements in the paragraph here in the original liner notes, the music nobody knows, are quite illuminating about the time. He said, “The music of these hot musicians and their talented colleagues must first be considered as music. It is not, as ignorant people contend, a sort of anarchy in music.”
